name: Liam Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we aren't selling anything. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Honestly, it's a mix of lectures I half-attend and a lot of time in the flat with a laptop and three monitors, which I'm not proud of. I study computer science, and Saturdays and Tuesday evenings I work at Spoke and Chain, a bike shop. I also sell little automation scripts to local businesses, like a script that sorts a cafe's orders into a sheet. I use AI tools all day, every day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did the script business start?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A friend's mum owns a nail salon, and she was typing bookings into three places. I built her a thing in an afternoon with an AI assistant and she gave me eighty pounds and a free manicure, which I declined. Now I've got four small clients. It's not much, but it's more than the bike shop pays per hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's about what I expected, and I'd stop pretending to be shocked by every new announcement. Even if it's hype, my little scripts still work for small businesses. I'd say it in the group chat, and then I'd move on to arguing about football.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be fine. My plan stays the same: finish my degree, keep the side business, get a placement. My parents pay part of my rent, and my bike shop job and scripts cover the rest. There's nothing scary about a world that just ticks along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going. More clients for the scripts, maybe ten by summer. I'd keep working at the bike shop, because I like the people there. And I'd apply for a placement at a software firm in the spring, with my side business on my CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Properly calm. It's like a day off from the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd double down on small clients. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably double down on small business clients. If the big hype fades, the practical stuff is what's left, and practical is where I make money. The nail salon, the cafe, a physio clinic, all with tiny jobs that need doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does this world look for your parents' work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad drives for a taxi firm and my mum works in a care home. In this world, nothing changes for them either, which is a relief. Dad's back is bad, so I'd still like him to have an easier job someday, but that's separate.

say: I'd say it's **what I expected** and stop pretending to be shocked.
I'd tell friends my scripts still work for **small businesses**.
think: I'd be **fine**: finish the degree, keep the side business, get a placement.
A world that **ticks along** isn't scary.
do: Find more **script clients**, maybe ten by summer.
Keep the **bike shop** job for the people.
Apply for a **placement** in spring with my side business on my CV.
feel: **Calm**, like a day off from the news.
S0.quote: If the big hype fades, the practical stuff is what's left, and practical is where I make money.
fieldNote: Liam is **calm for solid reasons**: a side income, family help and a plan.
He talks lightly and jokes, but his business is real and growing.
His dad's bad back and taxi work show a **family worry** he keeps separate from his own plans.

steps.text: Sign six more small-business clients for scripts
Keep working Saturdays at Spoke and Chain
Apply for a software placement with my client list

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the first real shake-up of my lifetime, and I'd say it with a grin, but I'd mean it. Some jobs shrink, some are new, and the people who can use the tools win. I'd say that online and probably annoy some people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, one thing worries me. My side business is little scripts, and AI is about to make those easy for everyone. In a year, the cafe owner can do it herself with a chat window. So the thing I'm good at might stop paying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd change what I sell. Instead of scripts, I'd sell setup and support, like going in and sorting out the whole system and checking it works. People will pay for someone to take responsibility. And I'd keep learning the newest tools every month, because I'm the type who enjoys that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but it's an exciting kind. I've been in the middle of change before, like when my dad's firm switched to an app and he had to learn it overnight. I helped him and I liked it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your scripts might stop paying. What would you do instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thing I'd have to be honest about is that I'm not special. Lots of people my age use the tools, so my advantage isn't the tool, it's that I talk to small business owners and they trust me. That's the bit nobody can download.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by the trust you have with owners?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For my course, I'd guess the junior jobs get harder. Companies hire fewer coders when tools write the first draft. I'd look at roles around customers and systems, where you need to understand a business, not just code.

say: I'd say it's the **first real shake-up** of my lifetime, with a grin.
I'd say the people who can **use the tools** win.
think: My scripts could **stop paying** once anyone can make them with a chat window.
My real advantage is **trust**, not the tool.
do: Sell **setup and support** instead of single scripts.
Look for roles around **customers and systems**.
S1.quote: My advantage isn't the tool, it's that I talk to small business owners and they trust me.
fieldNote: Liam sees the threat to his **own side income** clearly and adjusts at once.
He names trust with local owners as his edge, which is a **grounded, honest** view.
His adaptive nature shows when he says he enjoys learning new tools every month.

steps.text: Sell full setup and support packages to cafes
Try one new AI tool a week
Apply for customer-facing systems roles for placements
Keep the Saturday bike shop shift

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, okay, buckle up. I wouldn't say it's a disaster, I'd say it's the biggest speed-up ever and we need to be careful. Two years is nothing, and I'd say that out loud even though I'm the kind of person who normally likes change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be properly scared. My business gets wiped out, my degree jobs may not exist, and my dad's taxi work would be at risk three years later when cars drive themselves. Every pillar I'm standing on is shaky at once. That is what scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to stay ahead of it, because that's my nature. I'd put everything I make into savings, drop my spending to nothing, and look for the weirdest and most hands-on thing I can do with the tools, like set-ups for care homes. I'd also talk to people who've been through big shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's a buzzing feeling, like having too much coffee. I'd sleep badly but I'd keep moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd talk to people who've been through big shifts. Who?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum's care home is a good example. It's people work, and she's brilliant at it, but the paperwork would go to software. I think care jobs last longest, but I'm not sure they'd pay well. I'd want to understand what happens to wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you raise money with your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably have a hard talk with my parents, saying let's put some money away now. Dad's not going to like me telling him what to do, so I'd choose a good moment, probably after a Sunday dinner.

say: I'd say **buckle up**: it's the biggest speed-up ever, and we need to be careful.
think: My business, my degree jobs and my dad's **taxi work** all look shaky.
Every pillar I stand on is **shaky at once**.
do: Put everything I earn into **savings** and drop spending.
Look for **hands-on set-ups** with the tools, like care homes.
Have a **money talk** with my parents.
feel: **Anxious**, a buzzing feeling, like too much coffee.
S2.quote: Every pillar I'm standing on is shaky at once.
fieldNote: Liam's confidence is real but is **shaken** when business, degree and family income all look shaky.
He turns to motion and tactics, and describes feeling like **too much coffee**.
He sees care work as lasting longer, but he's unsure about its pay.

steps.text: Put all script income into a savings account
Cut spending to rent, food and bike parts
Offer care homes tidy digital paperwork set-ups
Talk to Mum and Dad about a family emergency fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, five years is enough to get a lot done if you start early. I'd say it to my friends as a challenge: what are you doing with the time? And I'd share the stuff I find useful, like which tools actually work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel okay, even a little excited. I'd have two years in work after my degree, and my side business could grow in the meantime. I'm uneasy about 2031, but it's far enough off that I'd rather build than worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd graduate, take a job at a company that does business software, and keep the side business alive. I'd save about half my pay. Maybe I'd also try to get a small amount of equity somewhere, because if the world changes, owning part of something is better than just a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way. I'm a person who likes a deadline, and a five-year deadline is workable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would owning part of something look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad's taxi job would be the place to watch. With cars driving themselves around 2034, he'd be late fifties. I'd want him to have savings by then, or a move into some other role. I'd need to start that talk about two years in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about your dad's timeline?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also build a safety net of my own, like three months of expenses, and a few clients who'd stay. If everything shifts, those are what I'd lean on.

say: I'd say five years is **enough** if you start early.
I'd ask friends what they're doing with the **time**.
think: I'd feel **okay**, even excited, with two working years before 2031.
Owning **part of something** beats just a wage.
do: Graduate and take a job at a **business software** company.
Save about **half my pay** and keep the side business.
Build **three months** of expenses as a safety net.
feel: **Uneasy**, in a good way, since I like a deadline.
S3.quote: If the world changes, owning part of something is better than just a wage.
fieldNote: Liam prefers a **deadline to a surprise**, so five years feels workable.
He thinks about **ownership** and equity as protection, which is unusual for his age.
He names his dad's taxi job as the main family risk and plans a talk in two years.

steps.text: Join a business software firm after graduating
Save half of every pay cheque
Ask a startup for a small equity share
Plan a talk with Dad about his taxi work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, ten years is a long time and most of the things we're worried about now won't even be the real problem by then. I'd tell friends to enjoy their twenties and keep learning. I'd say it online with a meme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel pretty calm. Ten years lets me build a proper business, maybe one with employees. I'd be 28, and I could be running something or working at something I like, rather than hoping for a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, but I'd probably spend more time on the business than the course, as long as my grades hold up. I'd save, invest a bit, and try something risky in my early twenties, because that's when failing is cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of curiosity. If I'm honest, the long runway makes me want to try more, not less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might drop out for a year. What would make you do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think about whether to drop out for a year, if the business really took off. My parents would panic, so I'd need numbers to show them. I'd only do it if I had a year's living costs saved, and I'd say so in advance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your twin sisters about their future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My twin sisters, Aisha and Zara, are twelve. In ten years they'd be 22, just entering this world. I'd want to help them pick things that need people and judgement. And I'd tell them that nobody really knows, so be curious.

say: I'd say **ten years** is long and most current worries won't be the real problem.
I'd tell friends to **enjoy their twenties** and keep learning.
think: Ten years lets me build a **proper business**, maybe with employees.
At 28 I'd rather be **running something** than hoping for a job.
do: Finish the degree but spend more time on the **business**.
Save, **invest a bit** and try something risky early.
Consider a **year out** only with living costs saved.
feel: **Calm**, with curiosity. A long runway makes me want to try more.
S4.quote: The long runway makes me want to try more, not less.
fieldNote: Liam reads the long timeline as **permission to take risks**.
He sets a clear rule on dropping out: **a year's living costs**.
He thinks about his twin sisters' future with an honest note that nobody knows.

steps.text: Grow the script business to ten regular clients
Invest a small monthly sum in index funds
Save a year of living costs before any year out
Help my twin sisters pick subjects they like

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, because everything I stand on shakes at the same time. What would help is some kind of safety net for people in the middle, and honest guidance from universities about which jobs are still worth training for.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that people like me get called confident about all this. I'm confident about myself, but I'm not confident about my dad's job or my mum's care home. Being good with the tools doesn't mean I'm not worried for everyone else.

headlineQuote: I'm confident about myself, but I'm not confident about my dad's job or my mum's care home.
portrait: Liam is an **18-year-old** computer science student who uses AI tools daily and sells small scripts to local businesses.
He works at a bike shop and his parents, a taxi driver and a care home worker, **help pay** his way.
He is centre-minded and **adaptive**, jokes a lot and likes deadlines and a challenge.
His side income is at risk when the tools get easier, so he moves to **setup and support**.
He is calm when the pace is slow, and fears for his **parents' jobs** when it is fast.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario worries him most, because his business, degree and dad's work shake together.
whatWouldHelp: A **safety net** for people in the middle and honest advice from universities on which jobs are worth training for.
